def-cau-backdoor-criterion.title: Back-door criterion
def-cau-backdoor-criterion.html:
Let X and Y be nodes of a DAG. A set Z of nodes, containing neither X nor Y, satisfies the back-door criterion relative to (X,Y) if

  1. no node in Z is a descendant of X, and

  2. Z blocks every back-door path from X to Y (@def-cau-confounding).

Such a set is called a (back-door) adjustment set.

def-cau-confounding.title: Back-door paths and confounding
def-cau-confounding.html: A back-door path from X to Y is a path between them whose arrow at X points into X, X←⋯Y. The effect of X on Y is confounded if some back-door path from X to Y is open given the empty set, that is, contains no collider.

def-cau-d-separation.title: d-separation
def-cau-d-separation.html:
Let Z be a set of nodes. A path is blocked by Z if

  1. some non-collider on the path is in Z, or

  2. some collider on the path is not in Z and has no descendant in Z.

Otherwise the path is open given Z. Disjoint sets of nodes A and B are d-separated by Z (disjoint from both) if every path between a node of A and a node of B is blocked by Z.

def-cau-dag.title: Directed acyclic graph
def-cau-dag.html:
A directed graph on nodes 1,…,m is a set of ordered pairs (l,j), l≠j, drawn as arrows l→j. It is acyclic (a DAG) if no sequence of arrows leads from a node back to itself. In a DAG:

  1. l is a parent of j, and j a child of l, if l→j;

  2. a path between l and j is a sequence of distinct nodes, starting at l and ending at j, in which consecutive nodes are joined by an arrow in either direction;

  3. a path is directed (from l to j) if every arrow on it points towards j; then l is an ancestor of j, and j a descendant of l;

  4. an interior node c of a path is a collider on the path if both arrows of the path that meet at c point into it, →c←; every other interior node is a non-collider on the path.

The graph of a structural causal model has an arrow l→j iff l∈pa(j). It is acyclic because parents have smaller indices.

def-cau-potential-outcomes.title: Potential outcomes and average effects
def-cau-potential-outcomes.html:
Consider n units and a binary treatment. Unit i has two potential outcomes: yi(1), the response it would show if treated, and yi(0), the response it would show if not. With Ti∈{0,1} the treatment it actually receives, the observed response is Yi=Tiyi(1)+(1−Ti)yi(0).{#eq-cau-consistency}

The unit effect is τi=yi(1)−yi(0), and the average treatment effect of the n units is τ=1n∑i=1nτi=y¯(1)−y¯(0). When the units are instead drawn at random from a population, so that (Y(0),Y(1),T) is a random vector, the population average treatment effect is E(Y(1)−Y(0)) and the average effect on the treated is E(Y(1)−Y(0)∣T=1).

def-cau-scm.title: Structural causal model
def-cau-scm.html:
Let V1,…,Vm be random variables. A structural causal model (SCM) for them consists of

  1. for each j, a set pa(j)⊆{1,…,j−1} of indices, the parents of Vj;

  2. for each j, a function fj, and mutually independent random variables U1,…,Um, the disturbances, such that Vj=fj(Vpa(j),Uj),j=1,…,m,{#eq-cau-scm}

    where Vpa(j) is the vector of parents of Vj.

Each line of @eq-cau-scm is an assignment: it says how nature sets Vj, not merely that an equation holds. Solving the assignments in the order j=1,…,m writes every Vj as a function of U1,…,Uj. For a variable X=Vk and a value x, the intervention do(X=x) replaces the kth assignment by Vk=x and keeps every other assignment and every disturbance unchanged. The distribution of the variables in the modified model is the interventional distribution, and expectations under it are written E(Y∣do(X=x)). The model is linear if each fj(v,u)=cj+∑l∈pa(j)bjlvl+u with constants cj,bjl, and disturbances with mean zero and finite variance.

eq-cau-adjustment.html: E(Y∣do(X=x))=E[E(Y∣X=x,Z)],

eq-cau-bias-m.html: βX∣C=τ−abc1c2D,D=(a2+σX2)(c12+c22+σC2)−a2c12>0.

eq-cau-u-representation.html: τ^=u¯S−nn0y¯(0),ui=yi(1)+n1n0yi(0).

exm-cau-bad-controls.title: Three bad controls by simulation
exm-cau-bad-controls.html:
Take, with unit variances throughout:

  • a mediator with θ=0.5, δ=1.2, γ=1, so that τ=1.7 and βX∣C=0.5;
  • a common effect with τ=1, a=0.5, b=1, for which @eq-cau-bias-common-effect gives βX∣C=1−(1.5)(1)/2=0.25;
  • an M-structure with τ=1 and a=b=c1=c2=1.5, for which D=134⋅112−8116=20516=12.8125 and βX∣C=1−81205=0.605.

Over 4000 samples of n=400, the least squares coefficients of X without and with C average 1.700 and 0.499 for the mediator, 1.000 and 0.251 for the common effect, and 0.999 and 0.605 for the M-structure (Figure 25.5.2). In the M-structure the adjusted estimate is also slightly less variable (standard deviation 0.046 against 0.050), a reminder that a smaller standard error says nothing about bias.

exm-cau-eight.title: Choosing an adjustment set
exm-cau-eight.html:
Figure 25.4.1 shows a linear model with unit-variance disturbances and W2=0.8W1+U,X=0.7W1+0.6W3+0.9I+U,M=0.8X+U,Y=0.5X+0.6M+0.7W2+0.8W3+P+U, with a separate disturbance U in each equation and W1,W3,I,P parentless. Summing over the two directed paths, τ=0.5+0.8×0.6=0.98. The back-door paths X←W1→W2→Y and X←W3→Y are blocked by W1 or W2, and by W3, and M is a descendant of X. So a set is valid iff it contains W3 and one of W1,W2, and not M; I and P are optional.

The listing computes the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,Z) exactly from Cov(V)=AA⊤, with the factor σY⋅XZ/σX⋅Z that governs precision (see below), and the standard deviation over 4000 simulated samples of size n=500:

adjustment set valid coefficient of X σY⋅XZ/σX⋅Z simulated sd
none no 1.308 1.15 0.052
W3 no 1.150 1.16 0.052
W1,W3 yes 0.980 1.25 0.056
W2,W3 yes 0.980 1.06 0.047
W2,W3,P yes 0.980 0.80 0.036
W1,W3,I yes 0.980 1.69 0.076
W1,W3,M no 0.500 1.72 0.077
W1,W2,W3,I,P yes 0.980 1.17 0.052

Every valid set gives τ; the invalid sets leave a back-door path open or, with M, keep only the direct effect 0.5. Among valid sets the standard deviation varies by a factor of two (Figure 25.4.2).

exm-cau-freedman-lin.title: When adjustment hurts
exm-cau-freedman-lin.html:
A synthetic population of n=400 units has one standardized covariate, on which the response depends under treatment (β1=2.007) but not under control (β0=−0.009); τ=1.003. With β0≈0 and Sxx=1, the condition of part (c) reads pβ1(pβ1−2(1−p)β1)>0, that is p>2/3. Figure 25.6.1 compares n times the variance of each estimator over 20000 randomizations with the exact variances of the approximating fixed-coefficient estimators:

fraction treated difference in means Fisher (ANCOVA) Lin (interacted)
0.2 20.88 (20.81) 14.03 (13.87) 4.80 (4.73)
0.5 6.01 (6.02) 2.04 (2.03) 2.03 (2.03)
0.8 5.20 (5.20) 13.50 (13.37) 4.26 (4.23)

(simulated; values from @lem-cau-fixed-coefficients in brackets). At p=0.8 the analysis of covariance has more than twice the variance of the unadjusted estimate while Lin’s estimator still gains; at p=0.5 both cut it by two thirds.

exm-cau-twenty.title: All randomizations of twenty units
exm-cau-twenty.html: A synthetic population of n=20 units has τ=2.100, S12=12.129, S02=5.678 and Sτ2=1.698; the effect grows with yi(0). With n1=8 there are 125970 assignments, few enough to enumerate. Over all of them τ^ has mean 2.100 and variance 1.9043, which is @eq-cau-neyman-variance to every digit. Neyman’s V^ has mean 1.9892, too large by Sτ2/n=0.0849. The pooled least squares variance estimate averages 1.7055, below the true variance, because it gives the more variable treated arm the weight of the smaller arm (@exr-cau-pooled-se). Figure 25.2.1 shows the distribution of τ^.

exm-cau-visits.title: Clinic visits and health
exm-cau-visits.html: In a synthetic population, Z is the severity of a chronic illness, which nobody records; X is the number of clinic visits in a year; and Y is a health score measured at the end of the year. Sicker people visit more (α=1.5) and end the year less healthy (γ=−6), and each visit helps (θ=2). With σZ=σX=1 and σY=2, @eq-cau-confounded-slope gives β∗=2+(−6)(1.5)1.52+1=2−93.25=−0.769. In a sample of n=2000 people the least squares slope is −0.790: each extra visit goes with a lower health score. A second data set in which visits are assigned at random, which is an intervention on X, has least squares slope 1.999 (Figure 25.1.2). A health authority that capped visits on the strength of the first regression would harm its patients.

exr-cau-any-effect.title: C1
exr-cau-any-effect.html: Take cZ=cX=cY=0 and normal disturbances in @eq-cau-confounder-model, and let Σ be any 2×2 positive definite matrix, with entries v=Σ11, c=Σ12 and w=Σ22. Show that for every real θ there are values of (α,γ,σZ2,σX2,σY2), with σZ2>0, σX2>0 and σY2≥0, for which (X,Y)∼N2(0,Σ). Hence the observational distribution constrains the causal effect not at all: @exr-cau-observational-equivalence exhibits two values of θ compatible with one distribution, and in fact no value is ever excluded.

exr-cau-bias-amplification.title: B3
exr-cau-bias-amplification.html: Let U be unrecorded, X=πI+gU+UX and Y=τX+hU+UY, with I, U, UX, UY independent, VarI=VarU=1 and VarUX=σ2. Show that the slope of L(Y∣X) is τ+gh/(π2+g2+σ2), and that the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,I) is τ+gh/(g2+σ2). Adjusting for the instrument I enlarges the bias.

exr-cau-butterfly.title: C1
exr-cau-butterfly.html:
(Butterfly bias.) Let H1,H2,UC,UX,UY be independent with mean zero and variance 1, and let C=H1+H2+UC,X=H1+C+UX,Y=τX+H2+C+UY, so that C is at once a collider on H1→C←H2 and a common cause of X and Y.

  1. List the back-door paths from X to Y and say which are open when C is not conditioned on, and which when it is. Conclude that neither ∅ nor {C} satisfies the back-door criterion (@def-cau-backdoor-criterion).

  2. Show that the slope of L(Y∣X) is τ+57 and that the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,C) is τ−15. Adjusting for C reduces the bias and reverses its sign, so the two estimates bracket τ.

  3. Now change one arrow, replacing C=H1+H2+UC by C=H1−H2+UC and keeping everything else. Show that the two biases become 37 and 15: both positive, so the two estimates no longer bracket the truth.

There is therefore no “adjust and compare” rule that turns two biased estimates into bounds.

exr-cau-cancelling-control.title: C2
exr-cau-cancelling-control.html:
(A bad control that does no harm.) Let H be unrecorded, UX,UC,UY independent of it and of each other, Var(H)=Var(UX)=1, Var(UC)=σC2>0, and X=H+UX,Y=τX+H+UY,C=pH+qX+UC. The control C is measured after the treatment: it is a descendant of X and a collider on X→C←H→Y, so the advice of this section forbids it twice over.

  1. Show that the slope of L(Y∣X) is τ+12.

  2. Show that the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,C) is τ+σC2−pqp2+2σC2.

  3. Deduce that the adjusted coefficient is exactly τ when σC2=pq, for instance at p=q=σC2=1, and check the two extreme cases q=0 and p=0 against @exr-cau-descendant-only and against the idea of a proxy for H.

Why does this not overturn the advice?

exr-cau-classify.title: A1
exr-cau-classify.html: A study of the effect of a training programme (X) on earnings two years later (Y) considers adjusting for: (i) education before the programme; (ii) the job obtained six months after the programme; (iii) whether the person was still living in the region at the end of the study, which depends on both training and earnings; (iv) the day of the week on which the person applied. Classify each as a confounder, mediator, collider or irrelevant, under a plausible graph, and say which should be adjusted for.

exr-cau-collider-descendant.title: B1
exr-cau-collider-descendant.html: Extend the collider by D=C+UD, with VarUD=δ and all other variances one. Compute σXY⋅D and show that it lies between 0 and σXY⋅C, approaching them as δ→∞ and δ→0.

exr-cau-common-b.title: A1
exr-cau-common-b.html: With one covariate and a fixed common coefficient b, show from @lem-cau-fixed-coefficients that τ^(b,b) has smaller variance than the difference in means iff b lies strictly between 0 and 2c∗. What does this say about guessing a slope from a previous study?

exr-cau-descendant-only.title: B1
exr-cau-descendant-only.html: Let X=UX, Y=τX+UY and D=dX+UD, where D is affected by X but has no connection with Y. Show that the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,D) is τ, and that the asymptotic variance of the least squares coefficient is larger with D than without it by the factor (d2σX2+σD2)/σD2.

exr-cau-direction-identified.title: C2
exr-cau-direction-identified.html: The impossibility in @exr-cau-any-effect is a fact about normal disturbances, not about observational data. Let UX and UY be independent, each taking the values ±1 with probability 12, and let the mechanism be X=UX, Y=X+UY. Show that no linear structural causal model (@def-cau-scm) in which Y has no parents and X=c+δY+U, with U independent of Y, reproduces the joint distribution of (X,Y), whatever the law of U and whatever c and δ are. So here the direction of the arrow is visible in the data.

exr-cau-excess-mse.title: B1
exr-cau-excess-mse.html: Let (xi,yi), i=1,…,n, be any data with least squares slope β^. For a number b, let ℓb(x)=y¯+b(x−x¯) be the line with slope b through the means. Show that 1n∑i(yi−ℓb(xi))2=1n∑i(yi−ℓβ^(xi))2+(b−β^)21n∑i(xi−x¯)2, and deduce the ordering of the two observational mean squared errors in @exm-cau-visits.

exr-cau-four-units.title: A1
exr-cau-four-units.html: Four units have potential outcomes (yi(0),yi(1))=(1,4), (3,3), (5,9), (7,8). Two are treated by complete randomization. List the six possible values of τ^, and verify @thm-cau-randomized(a) and (b) directly.

exr-cau-front-door.title: C2
exr-cau-front-door.html:
When every adjustment set contains an unrecorded variable, an observed mediator can still identify the effect. Let U be unrecorded and put X=aU+UX,M=δX+UM,Y=γM+bU+UY, with U,UX,UM,UY independent of mean zero and variances σU2,σX2,σM2,σY2, all positive, and a≠0, b≠0.

  1. Show that neither ∅ nor {M} satisfies the back-door criterion relative to (X,Y), so @thm-cau-backdoor identifies nothing from the recorded variables (X,M,Y).

  2. Show that the slope of L(M∣X) is exactly δ.

  3. Show that the coefficient of M in L(Y∣X,M) is exactly γ, while the coefficient of X there is bκ with κ=aσU2/(a2σU2+σX2), and so is not the direct effect 0.

  4. Conclude that the product of the two estimable slopes is the total effect τ=γδ. This is the linear case of Pearl’s front-door criterion.

  5. Show that the construction is fragile: if M=δX+gU+UM with g≠0, the two slopes become δ+gκ and γ+bλ with λ=gσU2/(g2σU2+σM2), whose product is not γδ.

exr-cau-harm-region.title: B2
exr-cau-harm-region.html: In the setting of @exm-cau-freedman-lin, let β0=0, β1=β≠0 and Sxx=1, and write p=n1/n. Show that the excess @eq-cau-fisher-excess, multiplied by n, is (2p−1)2β2/{p(1−p)}, and that the analysis of covariance loses to the difference in means iff p>2/3. What happens if instead β1=0 and β0=β?

exr-cau-hc2.title: B2
exr-cau-hc2.html: In the regression of the observed Yi on 1 and the treatment indicator, the leverages are hii=1/n1 for treated units and 1/n0 for controls (@prp-proj-leverage). The HC2 estimate of 𝛃Cov(β^) is (X⊤X)−1X⊤diag(e^i2/(1−hii))X(X⊤X)−1. Show that its entry for the coefficient of T is exactly Neyman’s V^.

exr-cau-imputation.title: C1
exr-cau-imputation.html: Show that Lin’s estimator is the average over all n units of the difference between the two arms’ fitted regression lines: if 𝛃α^t+β^t⊤x is the least squares fit in arm t, then 𝛃𝛃τ^L=n−1∑i{(α^1+β^1⊤xi)−(α^0+β^0⊤xi)}. Relate each arm’s term to the regression estimator of a population mean in survey sampling.

exr-cau-invariance.title: C3
exr-cau-invariance.html:
In @eq-cau-confounder-model, suppose an outside agent sets X to a random value X~ with mean m and variance ν>0, independent of (UZ,UX,UY); this is do(X=X~), and the observational regime is not of this form.

  1. Show that in the new regime the line ℓ(x)=a+bx has mean squared prediction error E{Y−ℓ(X~)}2={k+(θ−b)m}2+(θ−b)2ν+γ2σZ2+σY2,k=cY+γcZ−a.

  2. Deduce that the minimum is attained exactly at b=θ and a=cY+γcZ, whatever the agent’s device is, and that the minimum value γ2σZ2+σY2 does not depend on the device either.

  3. Deduce that the observational line of @eq-cau-confounded-slope has excess error at least (β∗−θ)2ν, which grows without bound as the agent spreads X more widely, and that a line that is optimal under two devices with different means is the causal line.

The causal line is thus the only line that predicts well under every intervention; the regression line is optimal for one regime, the one the intervention destroys.

exr-cau-lin-residuals.title: B1
exr-cau-lin-residuals.html: Let 𝛃ei(t)=yi(t)−y¯(t)−βt⊤xi be the residuals of the finite-population regressions. Show that 𝛃𝛃Varτ^(β1,β0)=Se(1)2n1+Se(0)2n0−Se(1)−e(0)2n, Neyman’s formula with the potential outcomes replaced by their residuals. Deduce that the proportional gain over the difference in means is large when the covariates explain much of both potential outcomes.

exr-cau-mediator-confounding.title: B2
exr-cau-mediator-confounding.html: In the mediator model add an unrecorded U, with variance σU2, that affects both the mediator and the outcome: C=δX+gU+UC, Y=θX+γC+hU+UY. Show that βX∣C=θ−δghσU2g2σU2+σC2, so that adjusting for the mediator does not even recover the direct effect θ.

exr-cau-observational-equivalence.title: B3
exr-cau-observational-equivalence.html: Take cZ=cX=cY=0 in @eq-cau-confounder-model with normal disturbances, and suppose only (X,Y) is observed. Show that the parameter values (α,θ,γ,σZ2,σX2,σY2)=(1,1,0,1,1,1)and(1,0,43,32,12,13) give the same distribution of (X,Y), although X has an effect on Y in the first model and none in the second.

exr-cau-paths.title: A1
exr-cau-paths.html: A DAG has arrows A→X, A→B, B→Y, X→Y, X→C, Y→C and D→C. List every path between X and Y, mark the back-door paths, and say which paths are open given ∅, given {B} and given {C}.

exr-cau-pooled-se.title: B1
exr-cau-pooled-se.html: Let sp2={(n1−1)s12+(n0−1)s02}/(n−2) and V^OLS=sp2(1/n1+1/n0), the least squares variance estimate for the coefficient of T. Show that V^OLS=V^ when n1=n0, and that in general EV^OLS−EV^=(n−1)(n1−n0)(S12−S02)n1n0(n−2). Conclude that when the smaller arm has the more variable potential outcomes, the least squares variance estimate is smaller on average than Neyman’s, and it can be smaller than the true variance.

exr-cau-positivity.title: C1
exr-cau-positivity.html:
Positivity is not a technicality. Let Z be 1 or 0 with probability 12 each; let X be 1 or 0 with probability 12 each when Z=0, and X=0 whenever Z=1; and let Y=τX+λZ+ψXZ+UY, with UY of mean zero and independent of (X,Z). The graph is Z→X, Z→Y, X→Y, so {Z} satisfies the back-door criterion.

  1. Show that the average effect E(Y∣do(X=1))−E(Y∣do(X=0)) is τ+ψ/2.

  2. Show that the right-hand side of @eq-cau-adjustment is not defined, because the positivity condition of @thm-cau-backdoor(a) fails at z=1.

  3. Show that the joint distribution of (X,Z,Y) does not involve ψ at all, and that the least squares regression of Y on 1, X and Z nevertheless returns the coefficient τ exactly, in the population and in every sample in which the three covariate patterns occur.

What, then, is the regression’s answer an answer to?

exr-cau-randomized-precision.title: B3
exr-cau-randomized-precision.html: Suppose X is randomized, so it has no parents, and P is a pre-treatment cause of Y. Show that both ∅ and {P} are adjustment sets and that v({P})=(1−ρYP⋅X2)v(∅), where ρYP⋅X is the partial correlation of Y and P given X. Compare with @prp-dsn-precision.

exr-cau-reverse.title: B2
exr-cau-reverse.html: Let Y=c+UY and X=δY+UX, with independent disturbances of variances σY2 and σX2. Find the slope of L(Y∣X), the squared correlation of X and Y, and E(Y∣do(X=x)). Show that the squared correlation can be arbitrarily close to one while setting X has no effect on Y.

exr-cau-sharper-bound.title: C1
exr-cau-sharper-bound.html: Show that Sτ2≥(S1−S0)2, and hence that Var(τ^)≤S12n1+S02n0−(S1−S0)2n, a bound that is attained when yi(1) is an increasing affine function of yi(0). Propose a conservative variance estimator that is never larger than V^.

exr-cau-stratified.title: B1
exr-cau-stratified.html: Let X∈{0,1} and let Z take values 1,…,K. In a sample, stratum z has nz units, a fraction p^z∈(0,1) of them with X=1, and difference of mean responses δ^z=y¯1z−y¯0z. Show that the sample version of @eq-cau-adjustment for the effect E(Y∣do(X=1))−E(Y∣do(X=0)) is ∑z(nz/n)δ^z, while the coefficient of X in the least squares regression of Y on X and the K stratum indicators is β^X=∑znzp^z(1−p^z)δ^z∑znzp^z(1−p^z). When do they agree?

exr-cau-table-two.title: B2
exr-cau-table-two.html: In @exm-cau-eight, show that the coefficient of W3 in L(Y∣X,W1,W3) is 0.80, the coefficient of the arrow W3→Y, while the total effect of W3 on Y is 1.388. Which set of variables would one adjust for to estimate the effect of W3?

exr-cau-three-sets.title: A1
exr-cau-three-sets.html: In @exm-cau-eight, decide which of {W1,W2}, {W3,P} and {W2,W3,M} satisfy the back-door criterion, and explain the coefficients of X that the listing gives for them: 1.201, 1.150 and 0.500.

exr-cau-trek.title: C1
exr-cau-trek.html: Show from @prp-cau-path-tracing(a) that in a linear model Cov(Vj,Vk)=∑lωlajlakl. Interpret each term as a sum over pairs of directed paths from Vl to Vj and to Vk, and use this to compute Cov(X,Y) in the chain of @prp-cau-three-structures.

exr-cau-zero-slope.title: A1
exr-cau-zero-slope.html: In the model @eq-cau-confounder-model with θ=2, γ=−6 and σZ=σX=1, for which values of α is the observational slope β∗ exactly zero? What would an analyst who saw β∗=0 be tempted to conclude?

lem-cau-fixed-coefficients.title: Adjustment with fixed coefficients
lem-cau-fixed-coefficients.html:
For fixed b1,b0, put c=(n0b1+n1b0)/n and 𝛃𝛃c∗=(n0β1+n1β0)/n. Then:

  1. Eτ^(b1,b0)=τ;

  2. the variance is Varτ^(b1,b0)=Varτ^D+nn0n1[(c−c∗)⊤Sxx(c−c∗)−c∗⊤Sxxc∗].

In particular the variance depends on (b1,b0) only through c, and it is smallest, over all fixed coefficients, exactly when c=c∗, for example when 𝛃𝛃(b1,b0)=(β1,β0).

lem-cau-srs.title: Means of a simple random sample
lem-cau-srs.title_html: Means of a simple random sample
lem-cau-srs.html: Let u1,…,uN and v1,…,vN be fixed numbers with means u¯, v¯ and Suv=∑a(ua−u¯)(va−v¯)/(N−1). If S is a simple random sample of m of the indices, 1≤m≤N, with sample means u¯S and v¯S, then Eu¯S=u¯,Cov(u¯S,v¯S)=(1m−1N)Suv.

prp-cau-adjustment-precision.title: Adding a variable to an adjustment set
prp-cau-adjustment-precision.title_html: Adding a variable to an adjustment set
prp-cau-adjustment-precision.html:
Let Z and Z∪{W} both satisfy the back-door criterion, with all covariance matrices positive definite.

  1. If σYW⋅XZ=0, then v(Z∪{W})≥v(Z).

  2. If σXW⋅Z=0, then v(Z∪{W})≤v(Z).

prp-cau-confounded.title: Seeing and doing with a common cause
prp-cau-confounded.title_html: Seeing and doing with a common cause
prp-cau-confounded.html:
In the model @eq-cau-confounder-model:

  1. E(Y∣do(X=x))=cY+γcZ+θx, so the interventional slope is θ;

  2. the best linear predictor L(Y∣X) has slope β∗=θ+γασZ2α2σZ2+σX2;{#eq-cau-confounded-slope}

  3. the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,Z) is θ;

  4. if the disturbances are normal, E(Y∣X=x)=L(Y∣X) evaluated at x, so the slopes of seeing and doing differ whenever γα≠0.

prp-cau-confounding-bias.title: Confounding bias in a linear model
prp-cau-confounding-bias.title_html: Confounding bias in a linear model
prp-cau-confounding-bias.html:
In a linear structural causal model with disturbances of positive variance, let X=Vk, Y=Vj, and let τ=ajk be the total effect of X on Y. For each l, let dl be the sum over the directed paths from Vl to Y that do not pass through X of the products of coefficients (so dk=0, and dj=1 from the trivial path of Y to itself).

  1. Y=τX+R, where R=∑ldl(cl+Ul) is the value of Y under do(X=0). Under do(X=x), Y=τx+R.

  2. The slope of the best linear predictor L(Y∣X) is τ+Cov(R,X)Var(X),Cov(R,X)=∑lωldlakl.{#eq-cau-backdoor-bias}

  3. If the effect of X on Y is not confounded, the slope of L(Y∣X) is τ.

prp-cau-exogenous.title: An exogenous cause
prp-cau-exogenous.html: In a structural causal model, suppose X=Vk has no parents, so that X=fk(Uk). Then a version of the conditional distribution of the other variables given X=x is their distribution under do(X=x); in particular, when E|Y|<∞, E(Y∣X=x)=E(Y∣do(X=x)) for almost every x (with respect to the distribution of X), and for every x with Pr(X=x)>0.

prp-cau-markov.title: Markov factorization and truncated factorization
prp-cau-markov.html:
Under this assumption:

  1. (V1,…,Vm) has density p(v1,…,vm)=∏j=1mpj(vj∣vpa(j)),{#eq-cau-markov}

    and pj(⋅∣vpa(j)) is the conditional density of Vj given V1,…,Vj−1, which depends on them only through the parents;

  2. under do(Vk=x), the other variables have density ∏j≠kpj(vj∣vpa(j)), evaluated with vk=x.

prp-cau-path-tracing.title: Path tracing
prp-cau-path-tracing.html:
In a linear structural causal model:

  1. I−B is invertible, V=A(c+U) with A=(I−B)−1, and Cov(V)=AΩA⊤;

  2. for j≠l, the entry ajl of A is the sum, over all directed paths from l to j, of the products of the coefficients on the arrows of the path (zero if there is none), and ajj=1;

  3. E(Vj∣do(Vl=x))=E(Vj∣do(Vl=0))+ajlx.

The number ajl is the total effect of Vl on Vj: the change in the interventional mean of Vj per unit change in the value imposed on Vl.

prp-cau-selection-bias.title: Selection bias
prp-cau-selection-bias.html: Let (Y(0),Y(1),T) be random with finite means and 0<Pr(T=1)<1. Then E(Y∣T=1)−E(Y∣T=0)=E(Y(1)−Y(0)∣T=1)+[E(Y(0)∣T=1)−E(Y(0)∣T=0)].{#eq-cau-selection}

prp-cau-three-structures.title: Chains, forks and colliders
prp-cau-three-structures.html:
Consider linear models with independent disturbances, VarUX=σX2>0 and so on, and write σXY⋅W for the partial covariance of X and Y given W (@def-mvn-partial-correlation).

  1. Chain X=UX, M=aX+UM, Y=bM+UY: Cov(X,Y)=abσX2 and σXY⋅M=0.

  2. Fork Z=UZ, X=aZ+UX, Y=bZ+UY: Cov(X,Y)=abσZ2 and σXY⋅Z=0.

  3. Collider X=UX, Y=UY, C=aX+bY+UC: Cov(X,Y)=0 and σXY⋅C=−abσX2σY2a2σX2+b2σY2+σC2.{#eq-cau-collider-partial}

With normal disturbances, a zero partial covariance means conditional independence (@prp-mvn-partial-meaning), so in (a) and (b) X and Y are dependent but conditionally independent given the middle node, and in (c) they are independent but, if ab≠0, conditionally dependent given C.

thm-cau-adjustment.title: Regression adjustment in a completely randomized experiment
thm-cau-adjustment.title_html: Regression adjustment in a completely randomized experiment
thm-cau-adjustment.html:
Under (A1)–(A3), let 𝛃𝛃bn=(n1β1+n0β0)/n.

  1. 𝛃𝛃β^t−βt→0 for t=0,1, and 𝛃β^p−bn→0, in probability.

  2. 𝛃𝛃n{τ^L−τ^(β1,β0)}→0 and n{τ^F−τ^(bn,bn)}→0 in probability. So, to order n−1/2, Lin’s estimator behaves like the optimal fixed-coefficient estimator and Fisher’s like the fixed-coefficient estimator with the common coefficient bn.

  3. The variances of these approximating estimators satisfy 𝛃𝛃Varτ^(β1,β0)≤Varτ^(b,b)for every b, in particular 𝛃𝛃Varτ^(β1,β0)≤Varτ^D; and 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃Varτ^(bn,bn)−Varτ^(β1,β0)=(n1−n0)2nn0n1(β1−β0)⊤Sxx(β1−β0),{#eq-cau-fisher-excess}

    which is zero iff n1=n0 or 𝛃𝛃β1=β0. Fisher’s approximating estimator has larger variance than the difference in means iff bn⊤Sxxbn>2bn⊤Sxxc∗.

thm-cau-backdoor.title: Back-door adjustment
thm-cau-backdoor.html:
Let V follow a structural causal model with graph G, let X and Y be two of its variables, and let Z be the vector of the variables in a set Z of other nodes.

  1. Adjustment formula. Suppose X takes finitely many values, Pr(X=x∣Z)>0 with probability one, E|Y(x)|<∞, and Y(x) is conditionally independent of X given Z. Then E(Y∣do(X=x))=E[E(Y∣X=x,Z)],{#eq-cau-adjustment}

    where the outer expectation is over the distribution of Z.

  2. The criterion gives ignorability. If Z satisfies the back-door criterion relative to (X,Y), then Y(x) is conditionally independent of X given Z, for every x.

  3. Linear models. In a linear structural causal model whose disturbances have finite positive variances, if Z satisfies the back-door criterion, the coefficient of X in L(Y∣X,Z) is the total effect τ of X on Y. Consequently, for independent copies of V, the least squares coefficient of X in the regression of Y on 1, X and Z converges to τ with probability one.

The proofs of (b) and (c) below are complete when Z contains every parent of X; for general adjustment sets they are sketches, since the proof of (c) uses (b).

thm-cau-bad-controls.title: Bad controls in linear models
thm-cau-bad-controls.html:
In each model below the disturbances UX,UY,UC (and, in (c), the unrecorded variables H1,H2) are independent with mean zero and variances σX2,σY2,σC2>0 (and 1). Let τ be the total effect of X on Y. In every case the slope of L(Y∣X) equals τ, so the simple regression is consistent, while the coefficient βX∣C of X in L(Y∣X,C) is as follows.

  1. Mediator: X=UX, C=δX+UC, Y=θX+γC+UY. Here τ=θ+γδ and βX∣C=θ: adjustment removes the indirect effect γδ.

  2. Common effect: X=UX, Y=τX+UY, C=aX+bY+UC. Then βX∣C=τ−(a+bτ)bσY2b2σY2+σC2.{#eq-cau-bias-common-effect}

  3. M-structure: X=aH1+UX, C=c1H1+c2H2+UC, Y=τX+bH2+UY. Then βX∣C=τ−abc1c2D,D=(a2+σX2)(c12+c22+σC2)−a2c12>0.{#eq-cau-bias-m}

thm-cau-d-separation.title: d-separation and conditional independence
thm-cau-d-separation.html:
Let V follow a structural causal model with graph G, and let A,B,Z be disjoint sets of nodes.

  1. If Z d-separates A and B in G, then VA and VB are conditionally independent given VZ.

  2. If Z does not d-separate them, there is a linear structural causal model on G with normal disturbances in which they are conditionally dependent; in fact this holds for all edge coefficients and disturbance variances outside a set of Lebesgue measure zero.

thm-cau-randomized.title: Randomization and the difference in means
thm-cau-randomized.title_html: Randomization and the difference in means
thm-cau-randomized.html:
In a completely randomized experiment with n1≥1 and n0≥1, let τ^=Y¯1−Y¯0.

  1. τ^ is unbiased for the average treatment effect: Eτ^=τ.

  2. Its variance over the randomization is Var(τ^)=S12n1+S02n0−Sτ2n.{#eq-cau-neyman-variance}

  3. If n1,n0≥2, the estimator V^=s12/n1+s02/n0 has EV^=Var(τ^)+Sτ2/n≥Var(τ^), with equality iff the unit effects are all equal.

  4. τ^ is the least squares coefficient of T in the regression of the observed responses on an intercept and the treatment indicator.

  5. If instead the units are independent copies of (Y(0),Y(1),T) with T independent of (Y(0),Y(1)), 0<Pr(T=1)<1 and finite means, then E(Y∣T=1)−E(Y∣T=0)=E(Y(1)−Y(0)), and the average effect on the treated equals the average treatment effect.
